---
title: "Mode coupling, power spectra and the EFT of large-scale structure"
---

## Eulerian perturbation theory in a nutshell

Expand the Eulerian density in powers of the linear field,
$\delta = \sum_n D^n \delta^{(n)}$, and write each order as a convolution of
linear fields with a **kernel**:

$$
\hat\delta^{(n)}(\mathbf k) = \int_{\mathbf k_1+\dots+\mathbf k_n = \mathbf k}
F_n(\mathbf k_1,\dots,\mathbf k_n)\,\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k_1)\cdots\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k_n).
$$ {#eq-spt}

For gravity the kernels follow from the recursion of @goroff1986 [reviewed in @bernardeau2002]{{< src spectra::f_sym >}}{{< test spt_kernels "kernels" >}};
the second-order one is

$$
F_2(\mathbf k_1,\mathbf k_2) = \frac57 + \frac12\,\frac{\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf k_2}{k_1k_2}\left(\frac{k_1}{k_2}+\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right)
+ \frac27\,\frac{(\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf k_2)^2}{k_1^2k_2^2},
$$ {#eq-f2}

or in real space $\delta^{(2)} = \tfrac57\delta_0^2 + \nabla\delta_0\cdot\nabla\varphi + \tfrac27\varphi_{,ij}\varphi_{,ij}$.
For the Zel'dovich / Burgers dynamics of [Chapter 5](05-zeldovich.qmd) the
kernels are simpler and factorize{{< src spectra::f_za >}},

$$
F_n^{\rm ZA}(\mathbf k_1,\dots,\mathbf k_n) = \frac{1}{n!}\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf k_i}{k_i^2},
\qquad \mathbf k = \sum_i\mathbf k_i ,
$$ {#eq-fza}

which is just the Taylor expansion of the determinant @eq-density-hc. The
difference $F_2 - F_2^{\rm ZA} = \tfrac{3}{14}\left[1 - \frac{(\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf k_2)^2}{k_1^2k_2^2}\right]$
is the tidal coupling that 2LPT adds and Burgers' equation lacks.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it: two plane waves"}
In the laboratory choose the *two plane waves* initial condition with wave
vectors $\mathbf k_1$ and $\mathbf k_2$. The Fourier amplitude map of the
evolved density shows new modes at $2\mathbf k_1$, $2\mathbf k_2$ and
$\mathbf k_1 \pm \mathbf k_2$ growing like $D^2$ with amplitudes given by
$F_2$; at third order you will find $3\mathbf k_1$, $2\mathbf k_1 \pm \mathbf k_2$
and so on. Compare 1LPT (Zel'dovich kernels) with 2LPT and 4LPT, and both
with the Hopf–Cole solution: Hopf–Cole reproduces *all* Zel'dovich harmonics
at once because the exponential resums the series. Make the two waves
parallel and the tidal term switches off, so that the gravitational and
Zel'dovich harmonics agree. The *Kernels* section of the laboratory turns
this into a measurement: it reads the harmonic amplitudes off the Fourier
map and divides out $D^2$ and the initial amplitudes, so that what is
plotted *is* the kernel (@sec-viscous-kernels).

:::

## Viscous kernels: perturbation theory for the adhesion model {#sec-viscous-kernels}

A natural question for anyone who has met both the adhesion model and
Lagrangian perturbation theory is: *what are the perturbation-theory kernels
of Burgers' equation at finite viscosity, and how do they differ from the
gravitational ones?* Solving @eq-adhesion order by order in $\delta_0$ is
tedious. The Hopf–Cole transform makes it a three-line calculation, and the
calculation turns out to be the quantitative version of
[Chapter 4](04-two-spaces.qmd): the nonlinearity sits entirely in an
exponential and a logarithm, so the kernels are *cumulants*.

### The potential as a cumulant generating function

Start from the exact solution @eq-adhesion-hc written for the velocity
potential, $\Phi = -2\nu\ln\psi$ with $\psi = G_D * e^{\varphi/2\nu}$, where
$G_D$ is the heat kernel, $\hat G_D(k) = e^{-\nu k^2 D}$. Because $G_D$ is a
normalized Gaussian, the convolution is an *average* of $e^{\varphi/2\nu}$
over Lagrangian points $\mathbf q$ drawn from a Gaussian of variance
$2\nu D$ around $\mathbf x$. The logarithm of an average of an exponential is
a cumulant generating function:

$$
\Phi(\mathbf x, D) = -2\nu \ln\Big\langle e^{\varphi/2\nu}\Big\rangle_{\mathbf q\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf x,\,2\nu D)}
= -\sum_{n\ge1} \frac{\kappa_n[\varphi](\mathbf x, D)}{n!\,(2\nu)^{n-1}} ,
$$ {#eq-cumulant}

where $\kappa_1 = G_D*\varphi$ is the smoothed potential, $\kappa_2 =
G_D*\varphi^2 - (G_D*\varphi)^2$ its variance under the kernel, and so on.
Every term is exact in $\nu$; the series is in powers of $\varphi$, i.e. of
$\delta_0$. The structure is worth a pause: the $n$-th order term carries an
explicit $\nu^{1-n}$, while the $n$-th cumulant of a field sampled with a
kernel of width $\sqrt{2\nu D}$ vanishes like $\nu^{\,n-1}$ as the kernel
shrinks. The inviscid limit is a product of a divergence and a zero, and the
finite result it leaves behind is the Zel'dovich solution; everything beyond
it is the viscous correction we are after.

### First order: the propagator

With $\hat\varphi = -\hat\delta_0/k^2$ and $1+\delta = \det(\mathbf 1 - D\nabla\nabla\Phi)$
from @eq-density-hc, the linear term $\Phi^{(1)} = -G_D*\varphi$ gives

$$
\hat\delta^{(1)}(\mathbf k) = D\,e^{-\nu k^2 D}\,\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k) .
$$ {#eq-viscous-propagator}

The linear growth $D$ is multiplied by the heat-kernel damping: viscosity
erases linear modes beyond $k_\nu \sim (\nu D)^{-1/2}$. In the laboratory
this is the row $\mathbf k_1$ of the *Kernels* table, and it is the reason
the Hopf–Cole power spectrum falls below the sheet at high $k$ when $\nu$ is
raised.

### Second order: the viscous kernel

Expanding the determinant to second order,
$\delta^{(2)} = -D\nabla^2\Phi^{(2)} + \tfrac12 D^2\big[(\nabla^2\Phi^{(1)})^2 - \Phi^{(1)}_{,ij}\Phi^{(1)}_{,ij}\big]$,
and inserting the second cumulant,
$\Phi^{(2)} = -\tfrac{1}{4\nu}\big[G_D*\varphi^2 - (G_D*\varphi)^2\big]$,
gives $\hat\delta^{(2)}(\mathbf k) = D^2\!\int_{\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2=\mathbf k} F_2^{\nu}\,\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k_1)\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k_2)$ with

$$
F_2^{\nu}(\mathbf k_1,\mathbf k_2) = e^{-\nu(k_1^2+k_2^2)D}\Big[
F_2^{\rm ZA}
- \tfrac{k^2\,\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf k_2}{2k_1^2k_2^2}\,(1 - \mathcal W)\Big],
$$ {#eq-f2-viscous}

where $\mathcal W = \mathcal W(2\nu D\,\mathbf k_1\!\cdot\!\mathbf k_2)$ with
$\mathcal W(x) = (1-e^{-x})/x = \int_0^1 e^{-xs}\,ds$.

Three things are visible at a glance.

1. **The inviscid limit is Zel'dovich.** $\mathcal W(0) = 1$ and the
   prefactor tends to one, so $F_2^\nu \to F_2^{\rm ZA}$ of @eq-fza. The
   gravitational tidal term $\tfrac{3}{14}[1-\cos^2\theta_{12}]$ never appears:
   Burgers' equation has no Poisson equation, and no viscosity will generate
   one. Adhesion is not an approximation to 2LPT; it is Zel'dovich plus
   dissipation.
2. **Both legs are damped.** The prefactor $e^{-\nu(k_1^2+k_2^2)D}$ is the
   product of the two linear propagators @eq-viscous-propagator: the
   second-order mode is built from already-damped linear modes.
3. **The coupling itself is weakened.** $\mathcal W < 1$ for aligned waves
   ($\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf k_2 > 0$) and $\mathcal W > 1$ for anti-aligned
   ones, so viscosity suppresses the growth of the sum mode
   $\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2$ more than the difference mode. This term is
   the trace of the second cumulant: the heat kernel converts the
   *interaction* of two modes over the time $D$ into an average over the
   history of the damping, as the integral form of $\mathcal W$ shows.

Higher orders follow the same pattern. The $n$-th cumulant supplies
$F_n^\nu$, and in the limit $\nu\to0$ the cumulants collapse to the
factorized Zel'dovich kernels @eq-fza. The complete answer to the question
we started with is therefore: *the perturbation theory of the adhesion model
is Zel'dovich perturbation theory with every propagator and every vertex
dressed by heat-kernel factors*; the gravitational kernels differ by the
tidal and higher Poisson terms that Lagrangian perturbation theory adds order
by order ([Chapter 6](06-lpt.qmd)). Models that put the viscosity back into
the gravitational equations, such as the adhesive gravitational clustering
of @buchert2005 or the Eulerian extension of @menci2002, interpolate between
the two.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it: measure the kernel"}
Open the *Kernels* section with the two-plane-wave initial condition. The
table lists, for $\mathbf k_1$, $\mathbf k_1\pm\mathbf k_2$, $2\mathbf k_1$
and $2\mathbf k_2$, the kernel *measured* from the Hopf–Cole density and
from the sheet, next to $F_2^\nu$, $F_2^{\rm ZA}$ and the gravitational
$F_2$. Hopf–Cole follows @eq-f2-viscous at every $\nu${{< src spectra::f2_viscous >}} (the core test
checks it to $10^{-3}${{< test viscous_kernel_limits_and_two_plane_waves "to 10⁻³" >}}); the sheet at order 1 gives the Zel'dovich value and
at order 2 and above the gravitational one, $5/7$ for orthogonal waves
instead of $1/2$. Sweep $D$ at fixed $\nu$ and the measured points slide down
the dashed viscous curves; sweep $\nu$ at fixed $D$ and watch
$\nu k^2 D$ become the only variable that matters. Keep $D$ well below
$D_{\rm sc}$: third- and fourth-order harmonics contaminate the second-order
modes in proportion to $D^2$.

{{< lab "ic=w&D=0.2&v=fk" "Measure the kernel in the lab" >}}
:::

### The whole lattice at once {#sec-lattice}

Perturbation theory produces the harmonics one order at a time. For the
Zel'dovich dynamics the Hopf–Cole exponential produces them all at once, and
for plane-wave initial conditions it does so in closed form. Mass
conservation, $(1+\delta)\,d^dx = d^dq$, gives the Fourier transform of the
density as an integral over Lagrangian space,
$\hat\delta(\mathbf k) = \int d^dq\, e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x(\mathbf q)}$
for $\mathbf k\ne0$. With two waves the displacement is
$\boldsymbol\Psi = -D\big[\tfrac{A_1}{k_1}\sin(\mathbf k_1\!\cdot\!\mathbf q)\,\hat{\mathbf k}_1 + \tfrac{A_2}{k_2}\sin(\mathbf k_2\!\cdot\!\mathbf q)\,\hat{\mathbf k}_2\big]$,
and the Jacobi–Anger expansion $e^{iz\sin\theta} = \sum_n J_n(z)e^{in\theta}$
turns the exponential of a sine into a sum of harmonics:

$$
\hat\delta(n\mathbf k_1 + m\mathbf k_2) = \pm J_n(z_1)\,J_m(z_2),
\qquad z_i = A_i D\,\frac{\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf k_i}{k_i^2},
$$ {#eq-lattice}

with $\mathbf k = n\mathbf k_1 + m\mathbf k_2$ and zero amplitude anywhere else. This is the two-dimensional cousin of
Cole's series @eq-cole-series. The evolved field lives on the **lattice**
generated by the initial wave vectors; the small-argument limit
$J_1(z)\simeq z/2$ reproduces the second-order kernel
$2F_2^{\rm ZA}\,\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k_1)\hat\delta_0(\mathbf k_2)$ at
$\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2$, while at shell crossing ($A_1D = 1$ for a single
wave) the amplitudes along the ladder $n\mathbf k_1$ decay as
$J_n(n)\simeq 0.45\,n^{-1/3}$, the Fourier image of the $|x|^{-2/3}$ density
cusp of a forming pancake. The phases are locked: with initial phases
$\theta_1,\theta_2$ the harmonic $(n,m)$ has phase $-(n\theta_1+m\theta_2)$
plus a sign, a *linear* function on the lattice.

This explains what the Fourier panels of the laboratory show for a Gaussian
field once $D$ is not small. A smoothed random field is dominated by a
handful of long modes; each generates a radial ladder of harmonics with the
period of its own wave vector, and each pair generates the oblique lattice
$n\mathbf k_i + m\mathbf k_j$ of @eq-lattice, with phases that vary
linearly across it. The striking regularities in the amplitude map, straight
rows of bright modes with a fixed spacing running diagonally across the
$(k_x,k_y)$ plane, and the parallel fringes in the phase map, are these
lattices; the spacing names the generating mode, and the direction of the
rows names the pair. In the Hopf–Cole picture the same lattice is already
present at $D=0$ in $\hat\psi_0$ (compare the $\log|\hat\psi|$ panel), with
amplitudes $I_n(A_1/2\nu k_1^2)\,I_m(A_2/2\nu k_2^2)$; the heat equation then
damps the harmonic $(n,m)$ by $e^{-\nu|n\mathbf k_1+m\mathbf k_2|^2D}$, and
the logarithm converts the modified Bessel functions of $\hat\psi$ into the
ordinary ones of @eq-lattice. After shell crossing the geometry of
[Chapter 5](05-zeldovich.qmd) takes over: each straight wall of the
adhesion tessellation contributes a streak through the origin along its
normal, with the phase $e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x_{\rm wall}}$ varying
linearly along the streak, and each node a broad contribution with a linear
phase; pairs of walls or nodes a distance $s$ apart beat with a period
$2\pi/s$ in $k$. Phase coherence across $\mathbf k$ is, in both regimes, the
Fourier signature of mass that has been *moved coherently*: a displacement
in real space is a linear phase in Fourier space, and the nonlinear maps of
[Chapter 4](04-two-spaces.qmd) are the only place where that information is
written.

### Viscosity is a counterterm {#sec-viscous-eft}

Square the propagator @eq-viscous-propagator and expand for small
$\nu k^2 D$:

$$
P^{(11)}_\nu(k) = D^2 e^{-2\nu k^2 D} P_0(k) \simeq D^2 P_0(k) - 2\,(\nu D)\,k^2 D^2 P_0(k) .
$$ {#eq-viscous-counterterm}

This is exactly the form of the EFT counterterm @eq-eft, with
$c_s^2 = \nu D$. The lowest-order effect of a viscosity on the power
spectrum *is* a speed-of-sound term, and its sign is the one the fits
return: positive, a damping. The adhesion model is therefore a concrete
realization of the EFT bookkeeping, with two differences that are worth
keeping in mind when the next section fits $c_s^2$. In the EFT the
counterterm stands in for whatever the unresolved gravitational dynamics
does to the long modes, its value is fitted (or matched to simulations),
and its time dependence follows from the small-scale physics; in the
adhesion model the "stress" is a specific, known operator,
$c_s^2 = \nu D$ grows linearly with the clock, and the same operator fixes
every higher-order vertex through @eq-f2-viscous instead of leaving them
free. And where the EFT needs a cutoff $\Lambda\sim1/R$ to define the loop
integrals, the viscosity supplies a soft one of its own at
$k_\nu = (\nu D)^{-1/2}$: raise $\nu$ in the laboratory and the one-loop
fit of $c_s^2$ to the Hopf–Cole spectrum tracks $\nu D$ until $k_\nu$ enters
the fitting range.

## The power spectrum at one loop

Average over Gaussian initial phases with $\langle\hat\delta_0\hat\delta_0^*\rangle = P_0(k)${{< src spectra::power_spectrum_hat >}}{{< test grf_power_spectrum_matches_input "GRF spectrum" >}}.
To fourth order in $\delta_0$,

$$
P(k, D) = D^2 P_0(k) + D^4\big[P_{22}(k) + P_{13}(k)\big] + O(D^6),
$$ {#eq-1loop}

$$
P_{22} = 2\!\int\!\frac{d^dq}{(2\pi)^d}\,F_2^2(\mathbf q, \mathbf k-\mathbf q)\,P_0(q)P_0(|\mathbf k-\mathbf q|),
\qquad
P_{13} = 6P_0(k)\!\int\!\frac{d^dq}{(2\pi)^d}\,F_3(\mathbf k,\mathbf q,-\mathbf q)\,P_0(q).
$$

$P_{22}$ is the power *generated* at $k$ by pairs of modes; $P_{13}$ is the
loss of coherence of the original mode. The laboratory evaluates both{{< src spectra::one_loop >}}
integrals numerically for the actual input $P_0(k)$ (with its smoothing),
in 2D or 3D, with gravitational or Zel'dovich kernels, and overlays them on
the power spectrum *measured* from the evolved field. For the Zel'dovich
kernels $P_{13}^{\rm ZA} = -k^2\sigma_v^2 P_0(k)$ with the velocity dispersion
$\sigma_v^2 = \frac1d\int\frac{d^dq}{(2\pi)^d}\frac{P_0(q)}{q^2}$: the famous
over-damping of the Zel'dovich power spectrum.

### Measuring the spectrum without a grid

Depositing the sheet onto an Eulerian grid and transforming is convenient
but introduces a window, aliasing and, for point-sampled deposits, a white
noise floor. Two deposit-free routes are available in the laboratory. The
Fourier transform of a plane wave over a simplex has a closed form, the
Hermite–Genocchi identity
$\int_T e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^d x = d!\,|T|\;\exp[s_0,\dots,s_d]$
with $s_j = -i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf v_j$ the vertex phases and
$\exp[\cdots]$ the divided difference of the exponential{{< src direct::direct_spectrum >}}{{< test direct_spectrum_matches_exact_deposit_at_low_k "vs exact deposit" >}} (one extra repeated
node for a linear density profile), so $\hat\delta(\mathbf k)$ of the
piecewise-linear sheet can be summed exactly over all simplices on any
lattice mode: the "direct spectrum", which measures the sheet's own $k^{-3}$
facet tail without any grid artefact. Alternatively, write the density in
Lagrangian form, $\hat\delta(\mathbf k) = \int d^dq\, e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x(\mathbf q)}$;
for the smooth, spectrally refined map the integrand is a smooth periodic
function of $\mathbf q$ and the trapezoidal sum over the refined grid
converges exponentially. Evaluated as a type-1 non-uniform FFT, this
"NUFFT density"{{< src direct::nufft_density >}}{{< test nufft_density_linear_and_refined "NUFFT" >}} counts all streams, has no facets, and converges with the
refinement factor, which makes it the reference for the true spectrum of
the map. When comparing with deposited fields remember their windows: a
cell-averaged estimator (the exact deposits, the dual sheet) carries
$\prod_a \mathrm{sinc}^2(k_a\Delta x/2)$ in its power spectrum, already
$0.4$ per axis at the Nyquist frequency, and must be deconvolved before
it can be compared with a deposit-free spectrum; point-sampled sheets and
the direct and NUFFT spectra carry no window at all{{< src sheet::tophat_cell_window >}}{{< test tophat_deconvolution_matches_direct_spectrum "deconvolution" >}}.

## Sensitivity to the cutoff and the EFT counterterm

Both loop integrals extend to $q \to \infty$. With the smoothing filter they
are finite, but they *depend on the smoothing scale* $R$ (or cutoff
$\Lambda \sim 1/R$). Change $R$ in the laboratory and the one-loop curve
moves, while the true large-scale dynamics must not care about what we did
to scales we cannot resolve. The resolution [@baumann2012; @carrasco2012] is that the fluid equations for the smoothed
field acquire an effective stress tensor from the unresolved small-scale
modes, whose leading effect on the power spectrum is a **counterterm**

$$
P_{\rm EFT}(k) = P_{\rm 1\text{-}loop}(k) - 2 c_s^2(\Lambda)\,k^2 D^2 P_0(k).
$$ {#eq-eft}

The "speed of sound" $c_s^2$ runs with $\Lambda$ in exactly the way needed to
cancel the cutoff dependence of $P_{13}$, and its finite part encodes real
small-scale physics that must be fitted to simulations (or, here, to the
higher-order sheet solution). The laboratory lets you fit $c_s^2$ by least
squares over $k < k_{\max}$ and watch it change with $R$ and with the LPT
order used as the "truth". Fit it to the Hopf–Cole spectrum instead and the
counterterm becomes a known quantity: @sec-viscous-eft shows that a
viscosity $\nu$ is a speed of sound $c_s^2 = \nu D$.

## The one-point distribution

The power spectrum is the simplest *two-point* statistic; the simplest
*one-point* statistic is the probability distribution of the density itself,
$\mathcal P(1+\delta)$, measured on cells of a chosen size. Linear theory
predicts a Gaussian of width $\sigma$, which already fails qualitatively once
$\sigma \gtrsim 0.3$ because it assigns probability to negative densities.
Gravity instead piles most of the volume up at densities somewhat below the
mean (voids) and stretches a long tail to high densities (filaments and
nodes); in terms of $\ln(1+\delta)$ the result is close to Gaussian, which is
the lognormal model of @coles1991. The shape depends on the
smoothing scale: averaging over spheres of a few cells lowers the variance
and pushes the distribution back towards a Gaussian, the central limit
theorem at work. The laboratory's *PDFs* section compares the distributions
of all its methods at the grid scale and in top-hat spheres (discs in 2D){{< src spectra::tophat_smooth >}}{{< test tophat_smoothing "top-hat" >}}
of ten cells diameter. The sheet, which sums all streams, and the adhesion
solutions, which collect the same mass into thin walls, populate the
high-density tail differently, and the Zel'dovich approximation, which
underestimates the collapse, falls short of the $n$LPT tail.

## Phases, propagators and the cosmic web

The power spectrum discards the phases, yet the phases carry the cosmic
web: randomizing them while keeping $P(k)$ turns a web of filaments and
voids into a featureless Gaussian field. Two diagnostics in the laboratory
make the phase evolution visible.

**Phase maps.** The map of $\arg\hat\delta(\mathbf k)$ of the evolved field
compared with that of the linear field: on large scales the phases are
inherited from the initial conditions, on small scales they decorrelate.

**The cross-correlation coefficient**{{< src Cosmo::cross_spectrum >}} [closely related to the propagator of
@crocce2006]

$$
r(k) = \frac{P_{\rm lin\times NL}(k)}{\sqrt{P_{\rm lin}(k)\,P_{\rm NL}(k)}} ,
$$ {#eq-rk}

which drops from 1 at low $k$ to 0 where memory of the initial conditions is
lost. For the Zel'dovich dynamics it is a Gaussian, $r(k) \simeq e^{-k^2\sigma_v^2 D^2/2}$,
and for the adhesion model the viscosity adds further damping: compare the
two directly by changing $\nu$.

**Lattices and streaks.** The amplitude and phase maps themselves are not
random. Before shell crossing they are superpositions of the harmonic
lattices of @eq-lattice, one per pair of dominant initial modes, with
phases varying linearly across each lattice; afterwards they are dominated
by the streaks of the straight walls and the linear phases of the nodes of
the adhesion tessellation (@sec-lattice).

**Phase statistics.** Two further diagnostics turn these pictures into
numbers, and both have a literature. The *phase-only reconstruction*
[@oppenheim1981; @chiang2000; @coles2000] keeps the phases{{< src spectra::phase_only_field >}} and sets every
amplitude to one before transforming back. On the lattice of @eq-lattice
the phases are linear in $(n,m)$, so the sum over the lattice is a Dirac
comb on the lines $\mathbf k_1\cdot\mathbf x = -\theta_1$ and
$\mathbf k_2\cdot\mathbf x = -\theta_2$: the pancake positions. For a
Gaussian field the same map peaks on the walls and nodes of the evolved
web, with the contrast information gone, which is the cleanest demonstration
that phases carry positions and amplitudes carry contrast. The *phase sum*
over closed triangles,

$$
\theta(\mathbf k_1,\mathbf k_2) = \varphi(\mathbf k_1) + \varphi(\mathbf k_2) - \varphi(\mathbf k_1+\mathbf k_2),
$$ {#eq-phase-sum}

is uniformly distributed for a Gaussian field and develops a peak at
$\theta = 0$ as structure forms{{< src spectra::phase_sum_hist >}}{{< test phase_statistics_lattice_and_gaussian "lattice and Gaussian" >}}. @matsubara2003 derived its distribution from
the polyspectra, $p(\theta) \simeq \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\big[1 + b\cos\theta + \ldots\big]$
with $b$ proportional to the normalized bispectrum, and
@hikage2004 and @hikage2005 measured it in simulations and in SDSS
galaxies; see also @wolstenhulme2015 for the three-point phase correlation
function. On the lattice, $\theta$ is $0$ or $\pi$ exactly: the tree-level
bispectrum has zero phase because the kernels $F_2$ of @sec-viscous-kernels
are real, and the $n$-th cumulant of @eq-cumulant fixes the $n$-point phase
closure in the same way. That phases shift in proportion to $k$ times the
displacement was noticed early [@ryden1991; @scherrer1991; @soda1992], the
universal growth of phase correlations in simulations is documented in
@jain1998 and @watts2003, and the mechanism is the one written in
@eq-lattice: a coherent displacement is a linear phase.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it: phases"}
Choose the *phase-only reconstruction* panel in the laboratory for the
Hopf–Cole or sheet density. With two plane waves at $D$ close to
$D_{\rm sc}$ the map is a set of straight lines on the pancakes; with a
Gaussian field it is the skeleton of the web. In the Spectra section the
*phase sums* plot shows $2\pi\,p(\theta)$ for the selected fields: flat at
one for the linear field, peaked at $\theta = 0$ for the evolved ones, more
so as $D$ grows and when weighted by the amplitudes (the distribution of the
bispectrum phase). Raise $\nu$ and watch the Hopf–Cole peak soften: the
heat kernel damps the harmonics but does not unlock their phases.

{{< lab "o=2&D=0.8&v=fs&f=sheetx_fphaseonly.sheetx_fabs.sheetx_fphase.sheetx&ps=a" "Phases in the lab" >}}
:::

Everything in this chapter is a statement about the *same* field seen in the
two spaces of [Chapter 4](04-two-spaces.qmd): the real-space picture shows
walls, filaments and voids forming; the Fourier picture shows power flowing
from the peak of $P_0$ to high $k$, phases scrambling, and the smoothing
scale controlling how far the perturbative description can be trusted.
